heading: Deregistering a license

content:
An expired license allows changes for seven days after the licensed date ends in UTC. When the server reports use on too many hosts, there are 21 days to finish the migration or assign separate licenses. Rechecking does not restart either period.
Checks use https://www.virtualmin.com/api/license/client with product=cloudmin. The license must belong to Cloudmin; Virtualmin licenses are rejected. The server reports the expiry date, host allowance and host use. Migration grace starts when this host first observes use above that allowance.
If verification fails, the last verified license can remain usable for up to 21 days. An earlier expiry or migration deadline still applies. Check the host clock and HTTPS connectivity, then recheck the license. Missing or invalid cached state requires successful verification.
heading: Grace periods

content: Cloudmin blocks new changes through the web interface, API and CLI. Existing machines and services keep running. Inventory, guest connections, accepted jobs, scheduled backups and recovery remain available. Forms and buttons stay available under their normal permissions. content:
Install Cloudmin with the automated cloudmin-install.sh script. It is the only supported installation method; there is no manual package walkthrough yet. If you haven’t already, read the Download page first, as it covers the steps most installations need.
Development channel
There is no Cloudmin 10 stable repository yet. The installer uses the unstable channel. Expect changes between builds.
heading: Installation

content:
Download the script to the host and run it as root, using the toggles to add the flags that match your setup:
copy sudo sh cloudmin-install.sh Managed swap No swap Or download and run it in one step:
copy sudo sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://download.cloudmin.dev/cloudmin-install.sh)" Managed swap No swap The script configures the Cloudmin repository, installs the package groups, then runs Cloudmin-Config, which completes the host configuration and checks readiness. It shows the installation plan, including any swap change, and asks for confirmation unless --yes is given. Logs are kept privately in /root by default.
heading: Running the install script

content: Usage: cloudmin-install.sh [options] --hostname|-n name Set a fully qualified host name --no-package-updates|-x Skip the initial distribution upgrade --extra package[,package...] Install additional distribution packages --include plugin[,plugin...] Include optional configuration plugins --exclude plugin[,plugin...] Exclude plugins (required dependencies cannot be excluded) --setup|-s Configure repositories only --swap|-S size Managed swap size: MiB, K, M, G (or KB/MB/GB) --swap-only Change swap without installing Cloudmin --no-swap|-ns Leave swap unchanged --log-dir directory Directory for the installation log --yes|-y Accept the installation or swap plan --verbose|-v Show debug messages --version|-V Show installer version --help|-h Show this help
heading: Install script options

content: Without a size, the installer chooses swap from available memory, existing swap and disk space. --swap 4G sets a size, --no-swap leaves swap alone, and --swap 0 removes only installer-managed swap. The managed paths are /swap.vm and, on Btrfs, /swap.virtualmin/swapfile; unrelated swap is never removed. --swap-only changes swap on an already installed host without installing packages or configuring repositories.
heading: Swap

content: Cloudmin does not install or configure BIND or Postfix; no DNS or mail server is needed to run virtual machines. Install additional services separately and configure them through Webmin. All shipped configuration plugins run by default. Use --exclude to skip a plugin unless another plugin requires it; the final readiness check is required.
heading: Optional services

content: Packages. On Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, CRB and EPEL are enabled and the cloudmincore and cloudmin-kvm groups are installed. On Debian and Ubuntu, cloudmin-core and the native cloudmin-kvm-stack meta package are installed, with Ubuntu universe enabled for the Perl virtualization bindings. Dependencies install in one transaction; failures stop the installer. Configuration history. Etckeeper tracks changes in /etc. Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux need initialization and a daily timer; Debian and Ubuntu packages handle their own setup. Existing history is preserved. Libvirt. Modular daemons are preferred when virtqemud is installed, otherwise the stock libvirtd is used. The selected services and sockets are enabled at boot so guests, networks and pools marked for autostart come back after a reboot. An incomplete modular installation fails rather than falling back to libvirtd; the QEMU, network and storage units must all be present. An idle daemon may exit while its listening sockets remain available. An active monolithic installation is never switched to modular automatically; follow libvirt’s migration steps first. Storage and network. A default storage pool is prepared and tested with a volume creation and deletion. A persistent default NAT network is created after checking host routes, without touching the management interface. Firmware. Packaged EFI firmware is verified so UEFI guests can be created. Security. Webmin, nftables and Fail2ban are configured through Webmin’s APIs. SELinux stays enforcing. Readiness. Before reporting success, Cloudmin-Config boots a temporary isolated KVM inspection appliance with a three-minute timeout and a 2 GiB memory limit. A failed boot stops the installation and shows the end of the configuration log; already installed packages are not rolled back. The installer requires Cloudmin-Config 10.0.0 or newer, a Webmin with the systemd get_unit_state API, and the matching Cloudmin module, DEB meta packages and RPM groups. These are published together.

content:
Settings are grouped by purpose: host connection and overview, virtual machine lists and details, creation, remote connections, backups, snapshots, images, networking and storage. Choose a category to edit its settings. These settings apply to all Cloudmin users on the host without changing their permissions or the data collected.
You can set the libvirt connection URI, bridge confirmation timeout, maximum image file size, default SSH authentication method, remembered Remote Access tab, automatic SSH connection, Webmin connection warning, pre-generated passwords and host-managed SSH keys. Edit creation defaults in System Settings → Machine Templates and Resource Plans; administrators can override them on the creation form without changing the saved presets or existing virtual machines. Creation checks host capacity, available space and image requirements.
Choose columns for virtual machines, imported images, the image catalogue, networks, storage pools and volumes, backups, backup schedules and the host snapshot list. Names always remain visible. Virtual machine and imported image states, backup schedule status and snapshot history position also remain visible.
Choose which sections start expanded on creation and backup forms and virtual machine detail pages. Advanced image import options and healthy host details can also start open. Failed host requirements are always shown to host administrators. Collapsed sections can still be opened on the page.
Images, networking and storage remember the last selected tab by default, separately for each Webmin user. Links to a specific tab override the saved choice. With this setting off, images opens the imported image list; networking and storage open their overviews. Read-only users can use saved choices but cannot update them.
Image settings choose a default import pool and whether the catalogue shows the host architecture or all architectures. By default, pool selection is automatic and only the host architecture is shown. An unavailable preferred pool falls back to automatic selection. Snapshot notes appear in each virtual machine’s history by default; hiding them does not delete them.
heading: Module Configuration

content: Cloudmin does not change cloud-init’s host configuration, does not create public IP addresses, and does not configure the guest OS beyond what cloud-init and the optional guest setup scripts do. Unsupported custom interface configurations stay under Webmin’s Network Configuration module.
heading: What is not managed

content:
Cloudmin 10 is a rewrite of Cloudmin around libvirt, the standard Linux API for managing virtual machines. It supports QEMU/KVM and runs as a module inside Webmin, using Webmin’s authentication, navigation, permissions and UI widgets.
The goal is simple: install Cloudmin on a supported Linux system, choose or supply an image, and get a safe, manageable KVM virtual machine without manual host setup. Cloudmin is useful on its own and integrates with Virtualmin for people who run hosting inside their guests.
title: What Is Cloudmin 10

content: Libvirt is the only management layer. Cloudmin does not build raw QEMU command lines or scrape virsh output. Libvirt stores the virtual hardware, network and storage configuration, so virsh, virt-manager and Cockpit keep working on the same machines. KVM first. Xen comes later through libvirt’s libxl driver once KVM is stable. Cloudmin 9 stays available and maintained for Xen users until then. A short default path. Install, pick an image, create a virtual machine. Firmware, machine type, extra disks and NICs live under advanced settings. One shared core for GPL and Pro. Pro adds features on top; it is not a second copy of the application. Virtualmin fleet management moves out. Cloudmin Services is not carried forward; an optional Webmin module, Virtualmin Connect, is planned to replace it. No provider clutter. Docker, Podman, LXC, OpenVZ, VServer, Zones, Citrix, EC2, GCE and similar screens are removed. Explicit import. Existing KVM installations will be imported by a tool with a per-machine report, cutover and rollback, never by a package upgrade. That tool is still planned.
heading: What changed from Cloudmin 9

content:
Web UI cloudmin CLI External clients Versioned controller API Roles, inventory, jobs, policy, audit libvirt domains, networks, storage pools QEMU/KVM The Cloudmin backend runs within Webmin. Virtual machine creation, power controls and management use a versioned API shared by the UI, the command line and external clients. Long operations such as image imports, creation, cloning, backups and restores run as background jobs with progress, resource reservations, cancellation at safe points and recovery after a restart. A small SQLite database holds only these job records and short-lived password hashes; everything else keeps Webmin’s file-based configuration and audit log.
Downloads, host-file reads, checksum checks, disk inspection, SSH key validation, cloud-init seed generation, consoles and terminal relays run as separate processes without root privileges, each in a systemd unit with a temporary user ID. See Privilege separation.
heading: How it works

content: Images from a verified catalogue, URLs, uploads and host files, plus installer ISOs Virtual machine creation from templates and plans with cloud-init accounts and networking Virtualmin GPL and Pro installation inside new guests, with progress on the host Power controls, live CPU and memory changes, disks, NICs, boot settings and media Disk snapshots, full clones and full backups with restore and schedules SSH terminals, serial and graphical consoles, and guest Webmin through the host NAT, routed and isolated networks and guided host bridges Storage pools on directories, NFS and LVM volume groups, with volume inventory Delegated access per virtual machine and live status in the browser See the feature status page for what is planned, including Cloudmin Connect for multiple hosts, Cloudmin 9 import and Xen.
heading: What it manages today

content: Cloudmin GPL manages one host with an unlimited number of virtual machines. Cloudmin Pro currently adds custom guest setup scripts, cloud backup destinations and image capture, with tenancy planned. Multi-host placement, live migration and failover are planned for Cloudmin Connect, a separate product. See Professional Features.
heading: Editions

content: Download and install Cloudmin on a supported host Create your first virtual machine Delegate access to other Webmin users
heading: Next steps

content: This guide walks through creating a KVM virtual machine from a cloud image on a freshly installed Cloudmin host.
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine
title: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: Log in to Webmin as a host administrator and open Cloudmin. The overview shows the host checks; fix any failed requirement first. Nothing else is needed: the installer already prepared a default storage pool, a NAT network and the EFI firmware, and the image catalogue is built in.
heading: Before you start
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content:
Open Create Virtual Machine
Click Create Virtual Machine in the Cloudmin menu. The form is based on Virtualmin’s Create Virtual Server page: the first section is open and the rest start collapsed.
Enter the details
Give the virtual machine a name. Names do not need to be domain names or have DNS records. The guest hostname defaults to the name; tick the checkbox below the name to set a separate hostname. Choose a template and a plan. The built-in Default Template selects Rocky Linux 10 for the host architecture, and Default Plan gives 2 CPUs, 2 GiB of memory and a 20 GiB disk (1 CPU on a one-CPU host).
Set the login
Supply the initial password or SSH public keys required by the selected login method. Cloud images configure the account through cloud-init. By default Cloudmin also creates a separate host-managed SSH key for the browser terminal; Module Configuration controls this.
Review the summary
A summary below the selectors shows the image, any download still needed, CPU, memory, disk size, network, addressing mode and software. It updates when you change a preset or edit a field.
Adjust sections if needed
Image and storage, Resources, Access, Software, Network and Boot options hold the editable template and plan settings. Change the image, pool, network, addressing (DHCP or static IPv4 and IPv6, including a /32 address with an on-link gateway), guest packages and scripts, firmware or autostart here. Manual changes keep the selected preset.
Click Create Virtual Machine
Creation returns a job immediately and shows its progress. If the catalogue image has not been downloaded yet, the job downloads and verifies it first and caches it for later use. Cloudmin chooses the machine type, UEFI or BIOS, and the disk bus from the host and image settings, and gives the guest its own writable disk so the source image stays reusable.
Open the guest
When the job completes, the virtual machine page shows live power state, guest agent status, SSH reachability, addresses and resource usage. Use Remote Access for the SSH terminal, serial console or graphical console. The serial console shows boot output; the graphical console works even before the guest has a network.
heading: Create the virtual machine
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: The job removes the resources it created and reports any cleanup that still needs attention, so you can retry. Guest setup failures, such as a failed script or installer, keep the virtual machine and point at the log inside the guest.
heading: If creation fails
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: To install an operating system from an ISO instead of a cloud image, choose Installer ISO as the source. Cloudmin creates an empty system disk and attaches the ISO in a read-only CD/DVD drive. Complete the installation through the graphical console, then eject the ISO or set the system disk as the first boot device. See Installer ISOs.
heading: Installer ISOs
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: Choose a Virtualmin GPL or Pro template to install a complete hosting stack inside the new guest. Virtualmin requires a fully qualified hostname, a fresh supported cloud image, at least 2048 MiB of memory for a full installation (1024 MiB for minimal) and 20 GiB of disk. See Virtualmin templates.
heading: Virtualmin guests
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: The same creation runs through api.pl on the host or the HTTP API with a signed token. See Virtual machine API.
heading: From the command line or API
pageTitle: How to Create a Virtual Machine

content: Cloudmin uses Webmin users and module permissions. A host administrator sees and manages everything; a delegated user sees only the virtual machines assigned to them, with the actions you grant.
title: How to Delegate Access

content: Granting the Cloudmin module to a Webmin user gives host administrator access by default, and existing users without saved Cloudmin permissions keep it. Creation, cloning, hardware editing, deletion, snapshots, backups, jobs, images, storage, networking and Module Configuration all require a host administrator.
heading: Host administrators

content: Open Webmin → Webmin Users, select the user or group, and open the Cloudmin module permissions. Set Host administrator? to No. Select the virtual machines the user may view. Assignments use UUIDs, so renaming a guest does not change access. Without assignments, the user sees no virtual machines. Grant the actions the user may perform on those guests. Each is a separate permission: ordinary power controls (start, shutdown, reboot, suspend, resume, autostart); forced power controls (hard reset and forced power off); the graphical and serial consoles; the SSH terminal; guest password resets through the guest agent. Assignment alone allows viewing details and live status. Changes and connections need their explicit grants, and Webmin’s read-only mode blocks them even when granted. Webmin’s safe and negative permission defaults grant no virtual machine access.
heading: Assigning virtual machines to a user

content: The virtual machine details page with power state, guest agent, SSH reachability, addresses, disks, filesystems and transfer rates The permitted power controls and Remote Access tabs The password reset form, which requires a running guest with a responding QEMU Guest Agent and never stores the password The same actions through the API with their own token, limited to their assigned UUIDs Live status connections recheck permissions every 15 seconds and reload the page when they change. Console and terminal supervisors check every five seconds and close sessions when access is revoked.
heading: What delegated users get

content: The Webmin tab in Remote Access, which opens a Virtualmin guest through the host’s Servers Index proxy, is available only to the host’s root Webmin login and needs Servers Index permissions as well. Other users with creation permission can create virtual machines, but registration is skipped and their Remote Access page has no Webmin tab. See Webmin access.
heading: Guest Webmin through the host

content: Give delegated users only the other Webmin modules they need: Cloudmin permissions cannot restrict host access granted through another module or through SSH. Delegation covers existing virtual machines; self-service creation, project ownership and quotas are Planned for Cloudmin Pro.
heading: Limits

content: Machine templates and resource plans are the presets behind the creation form. A template saves image, storage, network, guest access, software and boot defaults. A plan saves CPU, memory and system disk size. Both fill the form, where administrators can still change every value for one creation.
title: Templates and Plans

content: Both pages are under System Settings in the Cloudmin menu. The template editor uses a section selector with Previous, Next and Save and Next controls; resource plans use a collapsible Basic plan details section. Both use Webmin’s standard form widgets, Webmin configuration files, host access controls, form tokens, locking and audit logging. Reading presets never creates configuration files.
heading: Where to find them

content:
Cloudmin ships Default Template, four Virtualmin templates (GPL and Pro, each with Apache or Nginx) and Default Plan. Default Template selects Rocky Linux 10 for the host architecture. Default Plan supplies 2 CPUs, 2 GiB of memory and a 20 GiB disk; on a one-CPU host it uses 1 CPU. The Virtualmin templates use a full installation by default; minimal installation remains available.
All presets can be edited or copied. Default Template and Default Plan cannot be deleted. Virtualmin and custom templates can be deleted when no existing virtual machine or pending creation uses them; deleted built-in templates stay removed.
heading: Built-in presets

content: Basic settings including the name, description and Require fully qualified hostname. Custom templates can require it independently of their name or software; Virtualmin templates always do. The rule applies to cloud images, not ISO installers. Image and storage: the source image, which can be a catalogue entry not downloaded yet, the installation source and the destination pool. Access: the initial username, the authentication method (password, SSH keys or both) and SSH keys. Network: the libvirt network or host bridge, DHCP or static addressing, gateways and DNS. Software: packages and Virtualmin installation options, including whether to add the guest to the host’s Webmin Servers Index. Preparation and final setup scripts require Cloudmin Pro. Pro Boot options: firmware, whether to start after creation and autostart. Scripts can be disabled, entered directly or read from a host file. Host file access follows Webmin’s global file permissions and configured Unix user. Templates store the paths; creation jobs copy the contents before allocating resources, and scripts run only inside the guest.
heading: Template sections

content:
Supplied descriptions explain the shipped settings. Changing a built-in template’s name or settings clears its supplied description; custom descriptions are preserved. Built-in Virtualmin template names update on save to match the edition, web server and PostgreSQL option, with a numeric suffix for duplicates. Manually renamed and copied templates keep their custom names, and Default Template is never renamed automatically.
Template descriptions are hidden on the creation page by default. Show template description? in Module Configuration can display nonempty descriptions always, or only when they differ from the template name.
heading: Descriptions and names

content:
The creation form always selects a template and a plan; API callers select them explicitly. Editing a preset affects future forms; existing virtual machines and submitted jobs keep their settings. Manual field changes keep the selected preset, and deleting a custom default selects the built-in default again. Module Configuration retains the display, password generation and managed SSH key preferences, which do not add fields to the form.
Templates store settings, not prepared disk images. To create machines from a prepared disk instead, use cloning or, in Cloudmin Pro, capture an image and select it in a template.
Custom preparation and final setup scripts require Cloudmin Pro. Pro Packages and Virtualmin installation remain available in GPL, including the Virtualmin Pro templates. Virtualmin Pro itself needs a separate guest license.
GPL shows script controls as disabled previews unless Pro advertising is hidden in Module Configuration. Existing saved scripts remain visible and read-only. Clear both scripts explicitly when saving a template to use it without Pro; other edits preserve them, and creation refuses active scripts without the Pro package.
heading: How presets apply

content: The Software section of a template or creation request can install packages, run scripts and install Virtualmin inside a new guest. Cloudmin tracks the work from the host and keeps the virtual machine if setup fails.
title: Virtualmin Templates and Guest Software

content:
Guest setup requires a cloud image and Start after creation. After cloud-init finishes, a dormant helper service inside the guest runs as root in this order: the preparation script, package installation, the optional Virtualmin installation, and the final setup script. Scripts use /bin/sh -e and can switch users for application work. A failed or interrupted step stops without repeating scripts and keeps the virtual machine, with the error naming the log location inside the guest.
Cloudmin connects to the guest over SSH with the host-managed key and verifies the guest’s SSH host key through the guest agent channel before sending any credentials. Progress appears in the creation job while other guests continue disk operations. Guest software setup requires managed virtual machine SSH keys to be enabled in Module Configuration.
heading: Guest software setup

content:
Cloudmin ships Virtualmin GPL and Pro templates with Apache or Nginx. They run the official Virtualmin installer inside a fresh guest with options matching the installer’s command builder:
Bundle: LAMP (Apache) or LEMP (Nginx) Type: full or minimal installation PostgreSQL: optionally installed alongside MariaDB Hostname SSL: request a certificate for the guest hostname Add to host’s Webmin Servers Index: register the guest for the embedded Webmin view, on by default Virtualmin needs a fully qualified guest hostname, a fresh supported cloud image, Internet access, at least 2048 MiB of memory for a full installation or 1024 MiB for minimal, and a 20 GiB disk. The creation form shows the installation phases: waiting for guest setup, downloading the installer, installing, then configuring Webmin access through the host.
When the installation completes, the job links to the guest’s Webmin through the host, or directly to https://hostname:10000/ when registration was turned off.
heading: Virtualmin templates

content: Pro credentials are supplied for each creation request. They never enter templates, cloud-init seed disks, review responses or public job records, and they are removed from the job record once the guest has accepted them. Clones and captured images replace the Pro license and repository credentials with a placeholder before boot, so each copy needs its own license or a manual downgrade to GPL; the source license stays unchanged.
heading: Virtualmin Pro licenses

content:
After Virtualmin installation, Cloudmin saves the initial guest username and password in the host’s protected Servers Index configuration, with private permissions and excluded from Webmin’s file-change and undo logs. The setup job deletes its copy of the password when setup ends. If no password was saved, Servers Index asks for the guest login and remembers it for the browser session.
Only the host’s root Webmin login can register guests or use the Webmin tab. Creations by other users skip registration. If registration fails, the virtual machine remains usable and the progress page shows a warning; choose Open embedded Webmin on the Webmin tab to retry. See Webmin access for the trust model.
heading: Webmin Servers Index registration

content: Package-only and script-only setups need no Virtualmin resources and work with any supported cloud image. Use them to install an agent, join a configuration management system or seed an application. Scripts run only inside the guest and can read the initial username from CLOUDMIN_GUEST_USER.
heading: Packages and scripts without Virtualmin

content: Select a virtual machine from the guest selector to open its details, actions and Remote Access above the host-wide navigation links. Everything below is also available through the API and command line.
title: Managing Virtual Machines

content:
The details page shows power state, guest agent status, SSH reachability, addresses, individual disks, guest filesystems, network interfaces, and disk and network transfer rates. Power state and inventory update through libvirt events over an authenticated WebSocket; browsers do not poll. CPU usage is normalized to the assigned CPUs, and memory usage comes from ten-second balloon reports and excludes reclaimable cache. Filesystem usage and guest OS details require the QEMU Guest Agent and refresh about once a minute.
Power state, guest-agent health, SSH reachability and application health are separate signals. A responding agent does not mean guest setup has finished, and an SSH banner does not mean the first boot is complete.
The overview totals writable data-disk capacity and mounted filesystem usage, excluding read-only media and cloud-init disks. Host disk-image allocation is not guest filesystem usage. When usage is unavailable or stale, summaries show the known capacity alone. Host administrators also see counts of active image imports and unfinished virtual machine jobs from all users.
One host collector shares status results among viewers. Each browser receives an initial snapshot and later changes over an authenticated WebSocket, with session and module permissions checked on connection and while it remains open. Hidden tabs keep their connection but pause updates and guest checks. The collector exits about a minute after its last subscriber leaves; it uses Perl and Webmin’s WebSocket proxy, without a Node.js service.
Visible detail and connection pages share guest-agent and SSH-banner probes because SSH has no libvirt readiness event. Checks back off from five to thirty seconds when SSH responds; the overview does not probe SSH for every guest. Visible pages also share one nonblocking libvirt resource batch every ten seconds. New guests enable ten-second balloon reports; the collector enables them for existing running guests without changing their RAM allocation or saved definition. Host process RSS is not a substitute for guest memory usage.
Filesystem and guest OS checks run in one worker, at most once per second across the host and normally once per minute for each guest. Libvirt events can trigger an earlier refresh; all viewers share the results.
heading: Details and live status

content: Start, shutdown, reboot, suspend, resume and autostart are the ordinary power controls. Hard reset and forced power off are abrupt and require confirmation and a separate permission. Live ISO insertion and ejection work on running guests.
heading: Power controls

content: CPU count and balloon memory can be adjusted on a running virtual machine. Offline settings cover the resource maximums, boot order and firmware. The page explains when a change needs the guest shut down and what still has to be done inside the guest, such as growing a filesystem after a disk was enlarged.
heading: Resources

content: Add extra disks, grow existing disks, attach or detach volumes, and change the CD/DVD media. New disks are QCOW2 files in directory, filesystem and NFS pools, or raw logical volumes in LVM and LVM-thin pools; LVM disks grow only while the machine is shut down. Free-space checks run before every disk operation. Deleting a virtual machine asks which disks to remove, checks shared storage, and recovers an interrupted deletion the next time a host administrator opens Cloudmin.
heading: Disks and media

content: Add, change or remove NICs on a stopped guest, choosing a libvirt network or a host bridge. Cloudmin checks for duplicate MACs, duplicate managed addresses and missing networks before allocating resources.
heading: Network interfaces

content: Reset Password on Edit Virtual Machine changes an existing guest account through the QEMU Guest Agent. The form is always available to permitted users; saving requires a running virtual machine with a responding agent. Passwords are not stored in jobs or logs, and SSH authentication settings stay unchanged.
heading: Guest password reset

content: Snapshots save a disk state you can restore or delete later. Cloning copies a guest into an independent machine with a fresh identity. Backups write a full archive to local, SSH, S3 or Pro cloud destinations and restore it later. Create Image (Pro) turns a guest’s system disk into a reusable image.
heading: Snapshots, clones, backups and images

content: Creation, cloning, backups, restores, captures and offline hardware changes run as jobs. The progress page shows each step, the error if one fails, and whether cleanup is pending. Jobs reserve the virtual machine they work on, so conflicting operations wait. Unfinished jobs are recovered when a host administrator with write access visits Cloudmin; read-only and delegated visits never resume jobs.
heading: Jobs

content: Libvirt is the source of truth, so machines changed or created with virsh or virt-manager appear in Cloudmin. Deleting a guest with external tools does not run Cloudmin’s cleanup: remove its managed SSH key, serial logs and Servers Index entry separately in that case. Adopting guests defined outside Cloudmin with full management is Planned .
heading: Changes made outside Cloudmin

content:
Besides cloud images, Cloudmin can create a virtual machine that boots an installer ISO so you can install an operating system the traditional way.
Experimental
Installer ISO support is experimental. Alpine 3.24.2 ARM64 has passed a full installation and boot with the ISO ejected. Other installers still need testing.
title: Installer ISOs

content: Open Image Manager and import the ISO from an HTTPS URL, a browser upload or a file on the host. Imports accept installer ISOs alongside standalone QCOW2 and raw disk images. A host-file import must be readable without root; use a browser upload for a private file.
heading: Import the ISO

content: Open Create Virtual Machine and choose Installer ISO as the installation source in Image and storage. Pick the imported ISO. Cloudmin creates an empty system disk of the plan’s size and attaches the ISO in a read-only CD/DVD drive. Choose the firmware. UEFI is used where the host and image settings call for it; BIOS remains available for installers that need it. Create the machine. Cloud-init, the guest account settings and the managed SSH key are not used for ISO installations; access is configured inside the guest by the installer. Templates can require a fully qualified hostname, but that rule applies to cloud images only.
heading: Create the virtual machine

content: Open Remote Access → Graphical console to use the installer’s screen, keyboard and mouse. The console works during boot and without guest networking, and Webmin authenticates the connection without exposing a VNC password or port. When the installation finishes, eject the ISO from the virtual machine’s media controls or set the system disk as the first boot device, then reboot the guest.
heading: Install the OS

content: Install the QEMU Guest Agent inside the guest to get filesystem usage, guest OS details, password resets and live cloning support. Configure the guest’s serial port for a login prompt or boot output if you want to use the serial console. Cloudmin does not inspect ISO contents or configure the installed system.
heading: After installation

content: Cloning copies a virtual machine’s private writable disks into a new, independent machine. Choose Clone virtual machine from a guest’s action menu or Clone Virtual Machine on Edit Virtual Machine.
title: Cloning

content: Cloning works into directory, filesystem, NFS, LVM and LVM-thin pools; copies placed in an LVM pool become raw logical volumes. It requires libguestfs and its Perl bindings, bsdtar, and exactly one Linux installation that libguestfs can inspect. Prepared clones also require YAML::XS, enabled cloud-init inside the guest and one network interface.
heading: Requirements

content:
A stopped source is copied directly. For a running source, Cloudmin uses the guest agent to freeze filesystem writes, takes a temporary snapshot, thaws the source and copies the stable disks. File disks use an atomic external overlay that is merged back afterwards; LVM disks use native snapshots with a brief guest pause, and writes stay on the original volumes. A running source with both file and LVM writable disks needs a clean shutdown instead. The alternative for any source is a clean shutdown followed by copying and a restart. Filesystem freezing does not guarantee database consistency; stop databases or use their own tools for a consistent copy.
Both the source UUID and the destination name are reserved while the job runs. Cancellation and interrupted-job recovery restore the source before releasing either reservation. File and ordinary LVM pools need room for the full disk capacities and temporary snapshots, while thin pools allocate space as data is copied; these are included in the free-space checks, and output disks are checked for backing links before use.
heading: Stopped and running sources

content:
Prepared clone (new identity). Cloudmin resets the copied guest offline and supplies a new cloud-init seed before boot. A libguestfs task with networking disabled clears the machine ID, SSH host keys, DHCP leases, random seed and the cloud-init cache. The clone receives a new UUID, MAC addresses, console password, host ID and the access, network, boot and hostname settings you choose on the clone form, which reuses the creation form without installation media or software setup.
For Virtualmin guests, Cloudmin also updates Virtualmin’s management hostname, the Postfix hostname references and the management TLS certificate. Hosted domains and their certificates stay unchanged; application settings that use the source IP address still need review.
Keep guest settings and leave stopped. The copy preserves the machine ID, host keys, hostname, addresses and account credentials, and is left stopped with autostart disabled, so you can change its identity yourself before starting it beside the source.
Both modes assign a new host ID and replace Virtualmin Pro license and repository credentials with a placeholder before boot, using Virtualmin’s offline license API without contacting a server. The administrator must acknowledge that the clone needs a separate Pro license or a manual downgrade to GPL. The source license stays unchanged.
heading: Clone modes

content: UEFI variables can be copied from a stopped source and are stored in a file pool, even when the clone’s disks go to an LVM pool. Live cloning defaults to fresh variables, which do not preserve the source’s firmware boot entries. Passthrough devices, TPMs, shared folders, persistent memory and external device state cannot be copied; the clone and snapshot checks reject such guests. Linked copies and cross-host cloning are outside this implementation.
heading: Firmware and devices

content: Snapshots keep a restore point on the same machine instead of creating a new one. Backups use the same source preparation and recovery but preserve guest identity. Create Image (Pro) captures one system disk as a reusable image. Autoscaling from snapshot clones with pre and post hooks is Planned .
heading: Related features

content: Disk snapshots save the state of a virtual machine’s disks so you can return to it later. Open Snapshots from a guest’s menu for its history, or the host overview to see snapshots across all virtual machines.
title: Snapshots

content:
Snapshots cover private raw or QCOW2 file disks and managed LVM disks. On a running guest, Cloudmin asks the QEMU Guest Agent to freeze filesystem writes before the snapshot and thaws it afterwards, so the copy is filesystem-consistent. When the agent is not available you can choose an explicit clean shutdown first, or take an unprepared snapshot of the running disks. Filesystem freezing does not guarantee database consistency.
File disks get an external QCOW2 overlay managed through libvirt: new writes go to the overlay and the saved layer stays unchanged. LVM disks get a native snapshot volume instead: writes stay on the original logical volume, and Cloudmin pauses the guest briefly while the snapshot is created. A live LVM snapshot needs a disk cache mode that keeps no unflushed writes; disks created by Cloudmin use direct I/O. Classic LVM snapshots reserve room for a full disk’s changes in the volume group, while thin snapshots share their thin pool, so watch thin-pool data and metadata usage. One snapshot cannot mix file and LVM disks.
Snapshots are not supported for guests with shared folders, passthrough devices, TPMs or persistent memory, because their state cannot be captured; the check rejects them before any change is made. Up to 20 snapshots can be kept per machine, and snapshot history blocks disk attachment, removal and growth until it is removed.
heading: Creating a snapshot

content: Restore returns the disks to the saved state. Restoring an LVM snapshot copies the saved data back into the original logical volumes while the machine is stopped, and needs temporary space under /var/tmp for the largest disk’s full capacity plus 256 MiB. Delete merges a file snapshot’s overlay back into the disk and removes an LVM snapshot’s saved volumes; either way the current disk contents stay. Remove LVM snapshots before deleting a virtual machine. Both run as jobs with the usual reservations and recovery, and both respect the host’s disk-work queue so they do not race with clones or backups.
heading: Restoring and deleting

content: Scheduled snapshots and retention policies are Planned . Until then, use scheduled backups for unattended protection.
heading: Planned

content: Image Manager holds the disk images that virtual machines are created from: catalogue cloud images, your own imports and installer ISOs. Importing an image does not create a virtual machine; use Create Virtual Machine to choose a catalogue image or an existing import.
title: Image Manager

content:
The built-in catalogue lists cloud images of AlmaLinux, Alpine, Arch, CentOS Stream, Debian, Fedora, openSUSE, Rocky Linux and Ubuntu for the host’s architecture. Each entry records a stable ID, name, operating system, architecture, disk format, download size, minimum disk capacity, firmware and guest capabilities, release and support dates, and source URL. Catalogue downloads use HTTPS and are verified against the publisher’s SHA-256 or SHA-512 checksum manifest before import. Detached signature verification is Planned .
You can add custom catalogue entries with their own URL and optional SHA-256 checksum, and choose which columns the catalogue and import lists show in Module Configuration.
heading: The catalogue

content:
Imports use Webmin’s HTTP APIs, qemu-img and the system’s Sys::Virt Perl bindings. Downloads require the system CA certificate bundle.
Images can be downloaded from an HTTPS URL, uploaded from the browser or read from a file already on the host, into libvirt directory, filesystem and NFS pools. LVM pools cannot hold images; machines created in an LVM pool still take their image from a file pool. Imports accept standalone QCOW2 and raw disk images and installer ISOs; linked and encrypted QCOW2 images are rejected. Available space in temporary storage and the destination pool limits the size, and Module Configuration can set a maximum file size.
Downloads and imports run in the background with progress pages and batch operations. Temporary files are private, existing volumes are never overwritten, and a failed import removes the volume it created and reports any cleanup failure. A host-file import must be readable without root; use a browser upload for a private file.
heading: Importing images

content:
Templates can select a catalogue image before it is downloaded. A creation job reuses a verified copy or starts, or joins, an import in the destination pool before allocating guest disks. Downloads expose byte progress and do not hold the disk-work lock. Cancelling the creation leaves the shared import running; Image Manager can cancel it separately. Cached assets are reused without automatically refreshing rolling publisher URLs.
Cloudmin checks cloud image compatibility automatically. Custom cloud images without catalogue metadata are inspected read-only with libguestfs, its Perl bindings and YAML::XS.
heading: Images during creation

content: Images can be deleted individually or in bulk. Cloudmin checks that no volume still uses an image as a backing file before removing it, refreshing pools so entries removed outside libvirt do not block the check.
heading: Deleting images

content: With Cloudmin Pro, Create Image captures one Linux system disk of an existing guest as a standalone image in Image Manager. See Creating images from virtual machines.
heading: Captured images

content: Pro Create Image turns an existing virtual machine’s system disk into a reusable image in Image Manager. It is part of the Cloudmin Pro extension; the shared module rejects capture when the extension is absent, including direct API requests.
title: Creating Images from Virtual Machines

content: Choose Create image from a guest’s action menu or Create Image on Edit Virtual Machine. Enter an image name and a destination file pool (directory, filesystem or NFS), choose whether to remove login credentials for all local accounts, then choose whether to keep the source running with guest-agent preparation or shut it down cleanly before copying. Capture reuses the clone preparation, recovery and isolated guest preparation code, and requires libguestfs with its Perl bindings, YAML::XS 0.69 or later and bsdtar on the host. Host administrator access is required, and read-only sessions cannot submit a capture.
heading: Capturing an image

content: Capture supports one writable Linux system disk using virtio, with working cloud-init and an installation libguestfs can inspect. Cloudmin seed disks are omitted. Additional writable disks, attached installation media and read-only data disks are rejected, as are devices whose state cannot be copied, such as TPMs.
heading: Supported sources

content:
The result is a standalone QCOW2 image, also when the source disk is an LVM logical volume. Capture resets machine identity and cloud-init state, removes cloud-init logs, and replaces copied Virtualmin Pro license credentials with a placeholder. Remove login credentials? defaults to Yes: it clears password hashes, SSH credentials and default shell histories for all local accounts. No preserves those login credentials. Accounts, permissions, applications, data and other secrets remain, so captured images must stay private.
Virtual machines created from a captured image receive fresh host IDs, SSH host keys and access settings before boot, through the same prepared-clone path. Templates can select captured images like any other import.
heading: What the image contains

content: Cloning for a one-off copy with a fresh identity Image Manager for catalogue and imported images

content: Open Remote Access → SSH terminal on a running virtual machine to connect from your browser using its host-managed key or a guest password. The terminal requires Webmin’s Terminal module, Net::WebSocket::Server, OpenSSH, Python 3 and systemd with systemd-run.
title: SSH Terminal

content:
The connection form offers the guest’s current IP addresses, the SSH port, the username and the authentication method. The default username comes from the virtual machine’s creation settings when available, and the SSH service card shows whether SSH answers on the saved port before you connect. Choose the host SSH key created for this virtual machine or password login; passwords are typed into the terminal and are never saved or logged by Cloudmin.
On first use, the terminal asks you to confirm the guest’s SSH host key. Cloudmin remembers it for your Webmin account and that virtual machine, and blocks the connection if it changes.
heading: Connecting

content:
SSH defaults to port 22. After a successful login, Cloudmin saves that virtual machine’s port as the default for all Webmin users and for status checks. If the guest’s SSH port changes, enter the new port and log in once to save it. Failed logins leave the saved port unchanged.
Turn on Connect automatically when opening the SSH tab? in Module Configuration to skip the form. It is off by default. Each Webmin user has separate saved login settings for each virtual machine; automatic connection uses the saved port, username and authentication method, or the form defaults on first use. You still enter passwords and confirm host keys in the terminal. Failed or unfinished attempts return to the form and pause automatic connection until a login succeeds. Connection settings above the terminal opens the form at any time.
heading: Saved ports and automatic connection

content: By default, new virtual machines receive a separate host login key, added to the initial guest account through cloud-init. Module Configuration controls key creation and the terminal’s default authentication method; existing virtual machines are unchanged. Private keys stay in vm-ssh-keys under Cloudmin’s private module data directory with mode 0600, the terminal receives only its selected virtual machine’s key through systemd credentials, and the key is removed on creation rollback or when Cloudmin deletes the guest through its libvirt adapter. Deleting a guest with external tools does not run this cleanup; remove its saved key separately. These preferences do not add fields to the creation form.
heading: Host-managed keys

content: The browser relay and the SSH client run without root on the host, inside a systemd unit with a temporary user, no capabilities and no access to Webmin’s credential files. A root supervisor authorizes each connection, rechecks the session’s terminal permission every five seconds and stops the SSH process when you leave the page or the permission is revoked. Read-only Webmin accounts cannot open terminals.
heading: How it runs

content: Remote Access reopens your last selected tab, including when you open another virtual machine, with a separate choice for each Webmin user. Remember the last remote connection tab? is on by default in Module Configuration; links to a specific tab always override it, and an unavailable tab falls back to an allowed one.
heading: Remembered tabs

content: The serial and graphical consoles reach a local virtual machine without a guest network, SSH service or guest agent. Both require the virtual machine’s console permission, a local libvirt connection, Webmin’s Terminal module, Net::WebSocket::Server, Python 3 and systemd with systemd-run.
title: Serial and Graphical Consoles

content:
Remote Access → Graphical console shows the guest’s screen and lets you use its keyboard and mouse, including during boot and OS installation. It requires a VNC display on the guest. Webmin authenticates the connection and libvirt opens the display directly, so VNC passwords stay on the host and no public VNC port is needed. Use Fullscreen for a larger view and the keyboard menu to send shortcuts such as Ctrl+Alt+Delete or Ctrl+Alt+F1; their effect depends on the guest. Select the tab again after a connection closes.
Click inside the console and use Command + and Command - on macOS, or Ctrl + and Ctrl - on Linux, to scale the guest’s screen; Command 0 or Ctrl 0 restores the fitted view. Scaling keeps the guest’s proportions and does not change its resolution. Authentic Theme saves the zoom for your account.
Cloudmin ships the console client, layout and noVNC library, without noVNC’s separate application UI. Both consoles work with frame-based and SPA themes.
heading: Graphical console

content:
Serial console connects through libvirt to the guest’s PTY console or serial port, using the same permissions and non-root WebSocket relay as the graphical console; a root supervisor forwards bytes between the libvirt stream and the relay. New Cloudmin virtual machines have a serial port, but the guest OS must send boot output or a login prompt to it; Cloudmin does not configure that. Log in with a guest account and password; the managed SSH key is not used here.
Only one connection can use the serial port at a time. Close an existing connection before opening another, and leaving the page releases the port. An interrupted connection clears within about a minute, abandoned startup expires after 15 seconds, and both consoles close after 60 seconds without a browser response while protocol pings keep an idle connected session alive.
Zoom in the serial console changes the text size. Resizing the browser does not send new dimensions to the guest; if text wraps incorrectly, run stty rows 24 cols 80 inside the guest with the dimensions you need.
heading: Serial console

content:
Cloudmin enables libvirt serial logging on supported ports when creating a virtual machine or starting one that is fully stopped; a guest reboot or resume from a managed save does not enable it. Serial connections replay up to 64 KiB of recent output without sending keystrokes, which can show the existing login prompt or a partly typed command. The limited history may not fully restore a full-screen application.
Logs are private to root on the host at /var/log/libvirt/qemu/cloudmin-<UUID>-serial.log and contain all serial output, including echoed commands. Native virtlogd rotation defaults to 2 MiB per file with three backups, about 8 MiB per virtual machine. Each cold start clears the previous recording, and deleting the virtual machine through Cloudmin removes its logs. Cloudmin preserves custom console logs; its own recording requires stdio_handler = "logd", a positive max_size and 1–32 backups.
Guests without managed logging still show live output. If the console is blank, press Enter only when it is safe to submit any pending input.
heading: Recorded output

content: The Webmin tab in Remote Access opens a Virtualmin guest’s Webmin from the host, either directly in a new tab or embedded through the host’s Webmin Servers Index proxy. The embedded view works for guests on private NAT networks that your browser cannot reach.
title: Webmin Access

content: Only the host’s root Webmin login can register guests or use the Webmin tab, and Servers Index permissions apply on top, including read-only restrictions. Other users with creation permission can create virtual machines, but registration is skipped and their Remote Access page has no Webmin tab.
heading: Who can use it

content:
By default the tab shows a trust warning and two choices:
Open directly in new tab opens the guest’s own HTTPS address. Sign in with a guest Webmin account. Private addresses may be unreachable from your browser. Direct access uses neither the host proxy nor its saved login. Open embedded Webmin uses the host’s Servers Index proxy and signs in with the saved guest login. The embedded view replaces the choices, supports fullscreen, and follows the host’s light or dark palette and navigation color without changing the guest’s saved theme preferences. Clicking the Webmin tab again returns to the choices. To open registered guests in the embedded view immediately, set Show Webmin connection choices and a trust warning? to No in Module Configuration. Use it only when every registered virtual machine is fully trusted; changed IP addresses still require confirmation.
heading: Connection choices

content: Use the proxy only for fully trusted guests. The proxied pages share the host’s browser origin and your host session, so a compromised guest can use its Webmin pages to compromise the host and other virtual machines. Opening the proxy in another tab does not isolate it either.
heading: Trust warning

content:
Virtualmin templates enable Add to host’s Webmin Servers Index by default; turn it off in the template’s Software section to skip registration. After Virtualmin installation, Cloudmin saves the initial guest username and password in the host’s protected Servers Index configuration. The setup job deletes its copy of the password when setup ends, and Cloudmin excludes its changes to these login files from Webmin’s file-change and undo logs. Registration needs no extra guest account or SSH connection.
If no password was saved, for example when the guest was created with SSH keys only, Servers Index asks for the guest login and remembers it for the browser session. If the guest password changes later, update the saved login in the host’s Webmin Servers Index module.
If registration fails, the virtual machine remains usable and the progress page shows a warning. Choose Open embedded Webmin to retry after setup finishes; the same button registers an older or unregistered Virtualmin guest.
heading: Registration

content:
When the guest’s saved IP changes, an orange alert shows the old and new addresses and whether the new one matches the host’s static configuration for the guest or a DHCP lease for its MAC address. Addresses reported only by the guest agent or ARP are marked unverified. Confirm the address before opening the proxy; the saved entry is not changed until you do.
Cloudmin removes its Servers Index entry when it deletes the virtual machine.
heading: Address changes

content: Open Networking to see libvirt networks, host bridges, their addressing and the virtual machines attached to each. Cloudmin uses libvirt to manage virtual networks and guest interfaces, and Webmin’s network backends to create host bridges.
title: Virtual Networks and Bridges

content:
The installer creates a persistent default NAT network after checking host routes, without changing the host’s management interface. On the Networking page you can create more NAT, routed and isolated networks. Networks referenced by stopped or running guests are protected from deletion.
Virtual machine creation offers active libvirt networks and existing host bridges. It checks for duplicate MACs, duplicate managed addresses and missing networks before allocating resources. Cloud-init configures DHCP or static IPv4 and IPv6 inside the guest, including on-link gateway routes and /32 addresses, so guests on bridged or routed networks with provider-assigned addresses need no hand-editing after creation.
heading: Virtual networks

content:
A bridge lets guests join the upstream network and receive addresses from it. Each guest still needs a usable address from that network, and public access also depends on the upstream router, provider and firewall; creating a bridge does not allocate public IP addresses or configure the guest OS.
Guided bridge creation supports NetworkManager, Netplan and Debian ifupdown (which needs bridge-utils). Cloudmin reviews the selected standalone Ethernet interface, moves its saved addressing, routes and DNS to the new bridge, backs up the affected files and starts an independent systemd recovery timer before applying the change. You must confirm that the connection still works within the timeout, three minutes by default and two to fifteen minutes in Module Configuration. Unconfirmed changes are restored after the timeout, and also before networking starts after a reboot. Other host and virtual machine changes wait while a confirmation is pending. The timeout includes time spent applying the change. Changing it does not extend a pending transaction or disable recovery, including after a reboot.
For ifupdown, the interface must have an inet stanza, which may use manual on an IPv6-only host. If cloud-init regenerates the host’s Netplan files at boot, update its network configuration or disable its network rendering before converting the interface; otherwise it can restore the old port addresses after confirmation. Cloudmin does not change cloud-init’s host configuration. Unsupported custom interface configurations stay under Webmin’s Network Configuration module, and you should avoid editing the same host configuration elsewhere while a bridge change awaits confirmation.
Use Remove Bridge on an unused, persistent host bridge with one Ethernet port to move its current addresses, routes and DNS back to that port. Removal uses the same confirmation timer as creation; without confirmation, Cloudmin restores the bridge. First detach virtual machines, including stopped ones, from the bridge and its port, and update virtual networks that use either device. Multiple ports, dependent VLANs or macvlans, and unsupported custom settings require Webmin Network Configuration. Removal is also available through the CLI and API.
On Netplan hosts, Cloudmin keeps the DHCP client identity and requests the current IPv4 lease when moving settings between Ethernet and a bridge. During recovery, it requests the original address if restoring the files gives it a different lease. The DHCP server can still assign another address; use a DHCP reservation or static address to keep the host address stable.
heading: Host bridges

content: Offline management can add, change and remove NICs on a stopped virtual machine, attaching them to any network or bridge. The networking page and the details page show each interface’s MAC, source and discovered addresses.
heading: Guest interfaces
