--compression enables gzip; the default is an uncompressed archive. Allow space for disk copies, archive staging and temporary growth on the source. A filesystem-consistent backup does not coordinate transactions with other machines or replace application-specific backup steps.
Local and SSH destinations --dest-mode local writes to the absolute directory given by --dest-path. A mounted NFS or other network filesystem can be used as a local destination; mount and check it before starting the backup.
--dest-mode ssh transfers by SFTP. Supply --dest-host, --dest-user, an absolute --dest-path, and either --dest-password-file or --dest-key-file. The SSH port defaults to 22. A key option gives the path of a private key on the Cloudmin host; password options read the contents of a file. Unknown or changed server host keys must first be approved in Cloudmin’s backup form.
S3 destinations --dest-mode s3 uses --dest-bucket for the bucket and --dest-path for an object prefix. Supply the access key ID with --dest-access-file and the secret key with --dest-secret-file. Temporary credentials also use --dest-session-token-file.
--dest-region selects the region. --dest-endpoint selects an S3-compatible HTTPS endpoint; it must not include credentials or a path. --dest-ca-file supplies a CA bundle when needed. Supply provider credentials through the file options; the backup does not use the host’s cloud login settings.
Additional cloud destinations Cloudmin Pro also supports gcs, azure, bb, dropbox and drive. For Google Cloud Storage, Google Drive and Dropbox, the access and secret files contain the OAuth client ID or app key and client secret. Supply --dest-refresh-token-file as well. Google Cloud Storage uses a bucket and object prefix; Drive and Dropbox use --dest-path as the folder.
For Azure, --dest-account is the storage account, --dest-secret-file supplies its storage key, and --dest-bucket is the container. For Backblaze B2, --dest-access-file supplies the application key ID and --dest-secret-file supplies the application key; also select the bucket. Object stores use --dest-path as the prefix within that bucket or container.
Progress and recovery The command waits for the job by default. --no-wait returns its ID, and --json returns the final job record, or the initial record with --no-wait, without progress text. Completed backups appear in list-backups. If copying or transfer fails, inspect the job and use recover-job when cleanup is pending to finish restoring the source.
cloudmin backup-systems --name guest.example.com --dest-mode local \ --dest-path /srv/backups --compression cloudmin backup-systems --name guest.example.com --dest-mode ssh \ --dest-host backup.example.com --dest-user backup --dest-path \ /srv/backups --dest-key-file /root/backup-key cloudmin backup-systems --id MACHINE_UUID --dest-mode s3 --dest-bucket \ example-backups --dest-path cloudmin --dest-access-file \ /root/s3-access --dest-secret-file /root/s3-secret --no-wait Options:
--compression | --no-compression: Compress the archive with gzip. --dest-access-file file|-: Destination access file, or - for stdin. --dest-account value: Backup destination account. --dest-bucket value: Backup destination bucket. --dest-ca-file value: Backup destination ca-file. --dest-endpoint value: Backup destination endpoint. --dest-host value: Backup destination host. --dest-key-file value: Backup destination key-file. --dest-mode local|ssh|s3|gcs|azure|bb|dropbox|drive: Backup destination mode. --dest-password-file file|-: Destination password file, or - for stdin. --dest-path value: Backup destination path. --dest-port number: Backup destination port. --dest-project value: Backup destination project. --dest-refresh-token-file file|-: Destination refresh-token file, or - for stdin. --dest-region value: Backup destination region. --dest-secret-file file|-: Destination secret file, or - for stdin. --dest-session-token-file file|-: Destination session-token file, or - for stdin. --dest-subscription value: Backup destination subscription. --dest-user value: Backup destination user. --id uuid: Source virtual machine UUID. --name name: Source virtual machine name. --shutdown: Stop cleanly while copying and restart afterward.
heading: Creates a full backup of one virtual machine

content:
cloudmin inspect-backup [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] [--backup value] [--dest-access-file file|-] [--dest-account value] [--dest-bucket value] [--dest-ca-file value] [--dest-endpoint value] [--dest-host value] [--dest-key-file value] [--dest-mode local|ssh|s3|gcs|azure|bb|dropbox|drive] [--dest-password-file file|-] [--dest-path value] [--dest-port number] [--dest-project value] [--dest-refresh-token-file file|-] [--dest-region value] [--dest-secret-file file|-] [--dest-session-token-file file|-] [--dest-subscription value] [--dest-user value] [--filename value] Retrieves and verifies a backup before restoration. --backup selects a backup job ID from list-backups and uses its saved destination. To inspect an archive that is not in this host’s inventory, supply destination options and --filename instead. The filename is the archive’s name within the destination, not the destination directory itself.
The destination fields have the same meaning as in backup-systems, including credential files and SSH host-key approval. Supported archives are the complete backup files produced by Cloudmin, including gzip-compressed archives.
Inspection checks the manifest, checksums, disk information and saved machine definition. It does not create or start a virtual machine. The archive is downloaded or staged locally, so sufficient temporary space is required.
By default, waits for the inspection job. --no-wait returns its ID for get-job. Pass the completed inspection job ID, not the original backup ID, to restore-systems --inspection. Inspection downloads expire after one day; inspect the archive again if the staged copy is no longer available.
cloudmin inspect-backup --backup BACKUP_JOB_ID --json cloudmin inspect-backup --dest-mode local --dest-path /srv/backups \ --filename guest.tar.gz Options:
--backup value: Backup job ID from the local inventory. --dest-access-file file|-: Destination access file, or - for stdin. --dest-account value: Backup destination account. --dest-bucket value: Backup destination bucket. --dest-ca-file value: Backup destination ca-file. --dest-endpoint value: Backup destination endpoint. --dest-host value: Backup destination host. --dest-key-file value: Backup destination key-file. --dest-mode local|ssh|s3|gcs|azure|bb|dropbox|drive: Backup destination mode. --dest-password-file file|-: Destination password file, or - for stdin. --dest-path value: Backup destination path. --dest-port number: Backup destination port. --dest-project value: Backup destination project. --dest-refresh-token-file file|-: Destination refresh-token file, or - for stdin. --dest-region value: Backup destination region. --dest-secret-file file|-: Destination secret file, or - for stdin. --dest-session-token-file file|-: Destination session-token file, or - for stdin. --dest-subscription value: Backup destination subscription. --dest-user value: Backup destination user. --filename value: Archive filename in the destination.
heading: Verifies a backup archive before restoring it

content:
cloudmin restore-systems [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] --inspection value --pool ID|name --yes Restores one backup that has already completed inspect-backup. --inspection is the inspection job ID, and --pool selects the destination storage pool. --yes confirms restoring the archived machine and disks.
Restoration preserves the original machine name, UUID, MAC addresses, guest credentials and supported firmware state. It refuses a conflicting existing name or UUID even if that machine is stopped. This command is for recovering a machine; use clone-system when you need another machine with a new identity.
The destination host must support the archive’s architecture, firmware and saved network sources. Ensure those networks and bridges are available and that the pool has enough space. The restored machine is left stopped with automatic startup disabled, so its configuration can be checked before it joins the network.
The command waits for the restore job by default. --no-wait returns its ID. After success, use get-system, then start-system when ready. If restoration or cleanup is interrupted, inspect the job and use recover-job rather than submitting duplicate restores.
cloudmin restore-systems --inspection INSPECTION_JOB_ID --pool default \ --yes cloudmin restore-systems --inspection INSPECTION_JOB_ID --pool default \ --yes --no-wait Options:
--inspection value: Completed inspection job ID. --pool ID|name: Destination storage pool ID or name. --yes: Confirm this operation.
heading: Restores an inspected backup with its original identity

content:
cloudmin list-images [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists ready imported images and available catalogue images that can be selected for machine creation. The default table shows ID, name and format. --multiline or --json includes the available image metadata and compatibility information.
Imported images use their stored image ID. Catalogue entries use catalogue:IMAGE_ID; create-system downloads or reuses the selected catalogue image as part of creation. An unambiguous display name is also accepted by image-selection options, but use the ID when names are duplicated.
--name-only prints display names and --id-only prints selectable IDs. Catalogue entries can appear before their images are downloaded. Additional disks created with create-disk --image need a ready imported image, while create-system can use either source.
cloudmin list-images --multiline cloudmin list-images --id-only cloudmin list-images --json
heading: Lists imported and catalogue images

content:
cloudmin list-networks [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists available virtual networks and host bridges that Cloudmin offers for guest network interfaces. The default table shows a selection key, name, type and forwarding mode. Use it before create-system, add-interface or modify-interface.
A libvirt network key has the form network:UUID; a host bridge uses bridge:NAME. --id-only prints these selection keys, not just bare UUIDs. --name-only prints display names. Network options also accept a UUID or an unambiguous name.
--multiline and --json show additional reported network details. Selecting a network connects an interface to its existing configuration; this command does not create networks, configure host bridges or assign addresses inside an existing guest.
cloudmin list-networks --multiline cloudmin list-networks --id-only
heading: Lists usable virtual networks and host bridges

content:
cloudmin get-host [--multiline | --json] Shows host capabilities reported by Cloudmin, including relevant virtualization and image-handling support. Use this to check the host side of a creation or management requirement before choosing guest settings.
--multiline expands the capability fields, and --json returns structured data for scripts.
Use list-pools, list-networks and list-images for selectable resources. cloudmin api options returns the complete raw options response, including templates and plans, when a script needs those choices.
cloudmin get-host --multiline cloudmin get-host --json
heading: Shows host capabilities

content:
cloudmin create-image [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] (--name name | --id uuid) [--clean-credentials yes|no] --image-name value --pool ID|name [--shutdown] Captures a reusable image from the machine selected by --name or --id. --image-name names the new image and --pool selects its storage pool. This operation requires Cloudmin Pro. Use backup-systems instead to preserve a complete machine for restoration.
Source requirements The source must have a supported Linux installation with enabled cloud-init and one writable system disk. Detach installation media and additional read-only data disks first; Cloudmin’s own seed disk is omitted automatically. Unsupported devices or disk layouts are rejected before capture.
A running source needs a responding guest agent for a filesystem freeze and temporary snapshot. Alternatively, --shutdown stops it cleanly while copying and restarts it afterward. A source that was already stopped stays stopped. Cleanup changes are made to the independent image copy, not the source disk.
Account cleanup --clean-credentials yes is the default. It removes password hashes, SSH credentials and default shell history files for all local accounts in the image, including root. Accounts, ownership, permissions and application data remain. --clean-credentials no retains those login credentials and histories.
Custom history locations, application credentials and other secrets are not all discoverable, so review the image before sharing it. New-machine creation configures its selected administrator’s access separately.
Identity and licensing Regardless of account cleanup, Cloudmin resets cloud-init state, machine and host IDs, SSH host keys and cached network identity on the copy. Each new machine receives its own identity and network settings. Copied Virtualmin Pro license credentials are also removed locally without contacting license servers; each new machine needs its own license or a manual downgrade to GPL.
Result The image retains the source disk’s capacity, so new machines need a disk at least that large. The command waits for the capture job by default; --no-wait returns its ID. On success, the image appears in list-images and can be selected by create-system.
If capture is interrupted, inspect the job and use recover-job when needed to finish restoring the source and cleaning up incomplete output.
cloudmin create-image --name source.example.com --image-name base-server \ --pool default cloudmin create-image --id MACHINE_UUID --image-name private-copy --pool \ default --clean-credentials no --shutdown Options:
--clean-credentials yes|no: Remove all local accounts’ login credentials; defaults to yes. --id uuid: Source virtual machine UUID. --image-name value: New image name. --name name: Source virtual machine name. --pool ID|name: Destination storage pool ID or name. --shutdown: Stop cleanly while copying and restart afterward.
heading: Creates a reusable image from a virtual machine (Cloudmin Pro)

content:
cloudmin list-jobs [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists recent and unfinished jobs recorded by Cloudmin. Jobs include creation, software setup, hardware changes, cloning, snapshots, image capture and backup operations. The default table shows ID, name, operation, state and phase.
Use --multiline for details, or --json for scripts. Results exclude private requests, credentials and recovery backups. --id-only prints job IDs for later get-job, cancel-job or recover-job calls. --name-only prints job names, which need not be unique.
An unfinished job can reserve a machine or storage resource and block another change. Check its phase, error and cleanup status before resubmitting an operation. Leaving a terminal or timing out while waiting does not cancel a worker.
cloudmin list-jobs cloudmin list-jobs --multiline cloudmin list-jobs --id-only
heading: Lists recent and unfinished jobs

content:
cloudmin get-job [--multiline | --json] --job value Reads the current public record for --job. This is a job ID returned by a submitted operation or list-jobs, not a virtual machine UUID. It reports state, phase, recorded events, errors and available cleanup information.
The command reads once and returns; it does not keep following the worker. Use it after submitting an operation with --no-wait or after losing a terminal connection. --multiline expands details, while --json is suitable for polling from a script.
A successful status read does not itself mean the underlying job succeeded. Check the returned job state and error. A failed or cancelled job with cleanup pending may still hold resources; recover-job can retry that cleanup. For bridge changes, use get-bridge-status instead.
cloudmin get-job --job JOB_ID --multiline cloudmin get-job --job JOB_ID --json Options:
--job value: Job ID.
heading: Shows a job’s current progress

content:
cloudmin cancel-job [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] [--cleanup] --job value [--yes] Requests cancellation of the unfinished job identified by --job. Cancellation takes effect at a safe point in the worker; it is not an immediate process kill. Copying and backup operations may need to restore source disk state before releasing their reservations.
Started hardware changes cannot be cancelled after their first write. If such a change fails, use recover-job. Completed, failed or already cancelled jobs cannot receive a new cancellation request.
During guest software setup, ordinary cancellation leaves the created machine and changes already made inside it. --cleanup --yes explicitly requests removal of an eligible unfinished creation and its owned resources. This is not a general command for deleting a completed virtual machine.
By default, waits for cancellation and any cleanup. --no-wait returns immediately. Inspect the job afterward; a cancellation request is not proof that cleanup has finished. recover-job retries pending cleanup if the worker could not complete it.
cloudmin cancel-job --job JOB_ID cloudmin cancel-job --job JOB_ID --cleanup --yes Options:
--cleanup: Also remove an unfinished creation; requires –yes. --job value: Job ID. --yes: Confirm this operation.
heading: Requests cancellation at the next safe point

content:
cloudmin recover-job [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] --job value Reattaches or restarts work for the job identified by --job, including retrying cleanup marked as pending. It uses the original job’s recorded operation and resource identities rather than submitting a new request.
The result depends on the operation. Recovery can finish an interrupted hardware write, restore a source after copying, or remove incomplete creation resources. It checks the recorded state before proceeding and refuses unrelated changes. It cannot shrink a disk back after growth or recover data that was permanently deleted.
A failed job without pending cleanup is not automatically retried as a fresh operation. Likewise, recovery is not a way to rerun completed guest setup scripts. Inspect get-job --multiline for the failure and cleanup state first.
By default, waits until work or cleanup finishes. --no-wait returns immediately. Successful cleanup can leave the original job failed or cancelled with no cleanup pending; that records the original outcome while releasing its resources.
cloudmin recover-job --job JOB_ID cloudmin recover-job --job JOB_ID --no-wait Options:
--job value: Job ID.
heading: Resumes interrupted work or retries cleanup

content:
cloudmin discard-job [--multiline | --json] --job value Abandons the remaining edits of an eligible failed settings-update job while keeping disk growth that already completed. --job identifies that update. Use this only when you want to stop recovery of the remaining edits; recover-job attempts to finish them instead.
Cloudmin first checks that the original hardware definition is unchanged. It removes new disks allocated by the job only after verifying their identity and that nothing uses them. Completed disk growth remains because it cannot be undone safely.
When those checks pass, the job releases its reservation so the machine can be edited again. Conflicting changes or uncertain ownership block the operation. This command does not delete job history, cancel an active worker or undo other operations.
cloudmin discard-job --job JOB_ID Options:
--job value: Job ID.
heading: Keeps completed disk growth and discards the remaining failed edits

content:
cloudmin list-pools [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists all registered storage pools, including stopped pools and LVM-thin destinations. The table shows each pool’s name, UUID, backend, active state and available space. Free space is unavailable for inactive pools.
Use --multiline for pool settings, volumes and references, or --json for the full records. --name-only and --id-only print one name or UUID per line. Creating a virtual machine requires an active pool with a supported backend.
cloudmin list-pools cloudmin list-pools --json
heading: Lists active and inactive storage pools

content:
cloudmin list-volumes [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] [--pool ID|name] Lists volumes from active storage pools, with their pool, capacity, allocated space and owners. --pool accepts a UUID or a name that identifies exactly one pool, including LVM-thin destinations such as guests/thin. Omit it to list volumes across pools. Stopped pools cannot report their volumes.
--multiline and --json include ownership records and any reason deletion is blocked. A stopped virtual machine, imported image, snapshot or dependent disk can keep a volume in use. Cloudmin also blocks deletion when it cannot check these references. Listing volumes does not change storage.
cloudmin list-volumes --pool guests/thin cloudmin list-volumes --json Options:
--pool ID|name: Pool ID or unambiguous name.
heading: Lists storage volumes and their owners

content:
cloudmin list-volume-groups [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists existing local LVM volume groups that have no libvirt registration. Groups already registered are excluded even when their pool is stopped. Thin pools appear as storage destinations after their parent group is registered.
Create and extend groups with Webmin’s Logical Volume Management module or the LVM tools. This command lists groups without allocating or formatting disks. If discovery fails, it reports an error.
cloudmin list-volume-groups
heading: Lists LVM volume groups available for registration

content:
cloudmin create-pool [--multiline | --json] [--autostart | --no-autostart] [--group value] --name value [--path value] Registers a storage destination and starts it immediately. Supply a unique --name and exactly one of --path or --group. Directory paths must be absolute, have an existing parent and not overlap another pool. A missing directory is created; existing files and permissions are preserved.
--group names an existing LVM volume group. Registration does not format disks or create logical volumes. Its thin pools become separate destinations, named POOL/THIN_POOL. Startup with the host is enabled by default; use --no-autostart to disable it.
The command finishes before returning and shows the new pool record with --json. Running it again with the same name or volume group reports a duplicate registration.
cloudmin create-pool --name extra --path /var/lib/libvirt/extra cloudmin create-pool --name guests --group vg_guests --no-autostart Options:
--autostart | --no-autostart: Start the pool at host boot; defaults to enabled. --group value: Existing LVM volume group; cannot be used with –path. --name value: New pool name. --path value: Absolute directory path; cannot be used with –group.
heading: Registers a directory or an existing LVM volume group

content:
cloudmin start-pool [--multiline | --json] --pool ID|name Starts a stopped local directory pool with a saved registration. --pool accepts its UUID or a name that identifies exactly one pool. This includes pools unavailable for machine creation. The command reads the pool’s revision before starting it. If its settings change in the meantime, run the command again.
Starting does not create or format the directory or change its start-at-boot setting. This command does not start LVM pools.
cloudmin start-pool --pool extra Options:
--pool ID|name: Pool ID or unambiguous name.
heading: Starts a directory pool

content:
cloudmin stop-pool [--multiline | --json] --pool ID|name Stops a local directory pool while keeping its saved registration and all files. Stop virtual machines using the pool and finish or cancel pending operations and image imports first. Start the pool again before using it for new storage operations.
The command checks the current revision and finishes before returning. It does not stop LVM pools. Use unregister-pool --stop to stop an unused LVM pool and remove its registration after checking for host and guest use.
cloudmin stop-pool --pool extra Options:
--pool ID|name: Pool ID or unambiguous name.
heading: Stops a directory pool without deleting its files

content:
cloudmin set-pool-autostart [--multiline | --json] --enabled yes|no --pool ID|name Changes whether a local directory pool with a saved registration starts with the host. Supply --pool as a UUID or unambiguous name and --enabled yes or --enabled no. This setting does not immediately start or stop the pool.
The command reads and checks the current revision before saving. LVM registrations receive their start-at-boot setting during create-pool; this command manages directory pools only.
cloudmin set-pool-autostart --pool extra --enabled no Options:
--enabled yes|no: Whether to start at host boot. --pool ID|name: Pool ID or unambiguous name.
heading: Changes whether a directory pool starts at boot

content:
cloudmin delete-volume [--multiline | --json] (--review | --yes) --pool ID|name --volume value Permanently deletes one unused volume from an active local directory or LVM destination. Supply --pool and the exact --volume name. --review shows owners and any refusal reason without changing anything or requiring --yes.
Deletion requires --yes. The command reviews the volume, then sends its revision for a final check under the host storage lock. A replaced volume, new reference or pending operation prevents deletion. Host mounts, swap and Cloudmin snapshots also block deletion. Deleting the volume destroys its data and cannot be undone.
The command finishes before returning. To delete several volumes, run it separately for each volume and check each result before continuing.
cloudmin delete-volume --pool guests/thin --volume unused.raw --review cloudmin delete-volume --pool guests/thin --volume unused.raw --yes Options:
--pool ID|name: Pool ID or unambiguous name. --review: Show owners and any reason deletion is blocked. --volume value: Exact volume name. --yes: Confirm this operation.
heading: Deletes an unused storage volume after a review

content:
cloudmin unregister-pool [--multiline | --json] (--review | --yes) --pool ID|name [--stop] Removes the saved libvirt registration for a local directory or LVM pool. Files, logical volumes, volume groups and thin pools are preserved. Supply the parent pool’s UUID or unambiguous name with --pool. LVM-thin destinations cannot be unregistered separately.
--review shows references and any reason removal is blocked without requiring --yes. Removing the registration requires --yes and repeats the revision and reference checks. References from running or stopped guests, images, snapshots and dependent disks block removal, as do pending operations. Other inactive pools may need to be started so their references can be checked.
An active pool requires --stop. For LVM, stopping deactivates every logical volume in the group, including thin volumes. Cloudmin refuses to stop the group if its volumes are mounted, used as swap, open, or used by other block devices outside the group. Register the group again to use it in Cloudmin.
Use --stop --review to review both steps without changing storage. --stop --yes repeats the checks under the host lock, stops the pool and removes its registration. Without --stop, the pool must already be inactive.
If the volume group no longer exists, Cloudmin can remove its inactive registration after checking for references. It must be able to read the LVM inventory and confirm that the group is absent. An active pool or a failed inventory read still blocks removal.
A failed stop keeps the registration. If stopping succeeds but removing the registration fails, the error says the pool is stopped. Review it again before retrying.
cloudmin unregister-pool --pool extra --review cloudmin unregister-pool --pool extra --yes cloudmin unregister-pool --pool guests --stop --review cloudmin unregister-pool --pool guests --stop --yes Options:
--pool ID|name: Directory or parent LVM pool ID or name. --review: Show references and any reason unregistration is blocked. --stop: Stop the unused pool first; LVM deactivates the whole volume group. --yes: Confirm this operation.
heading: Removes a pool registration and keeps its data

content:
cloudmin list-bridges [--multiline | --json] [--name-only | --id-only] Lists host bridges outside libvirt-managed virtual networks. These bridges connect guests to the host’s existing network. Libvirt-managed NAT or routed bridges belong to their virtual networks and are not removal targets here.
The default table shows each bridge’s name, whether it is active, its addresses and its ports. --multiline and --json include saved-configuration and dependency details. --name-only and --id-only both print bridge names, such as br0.
Use remove-bridge --review to see whether a bridge can be removed and what settings would move to its Ethernet port. Active or recent bridge transactions are inspected separately with get-bridge-status.
cloudmin list-bridges --multiline cloudmin list-bridges --name-only
heading: Lists host bridges outside libvirt-managed networks

content:
cloudmin get-bridge-status [--multiline | --json] [--id value] Shows the current host bridge transaction, including its state and available confirmation or recovery information. Without --id, selects the current transaction. With --id, requires that specific transaction so a stale script does not act on a newer change.
The transaction ID is returned by bridge changes; it is not the bridge name or a normal background job ID. The result can be empty when there is no transaction. --json returns structured status for scripts, and --multiline expands human-readable details.
Use this after a connection interruption or remove-bridge --no-wait. A change awaiting confirmation must be kept with confirm-bridge before its deadline, or it is automatically rolled back. Private recovery files are not included in the response.
cloudmin get-bridge-status --multiline cloudmin get-bridge-status --id TRANSACTION_ID --json Options:
--id value: Transaction ID; omitted selects the current transaction.
heading: Shows the current bridge transaction

content:
cloudmin remove-bridge [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] --name value [--review] Removes an unused, saved host bridge with one supported Ethernet port. --name is the bridge name from list-bridges, not a virtual machine name. The bridge’s current addresses, routes and DNS settings move back to its Ethernet port.
Cloudmin supports bridge removal with NetworkManager, Netplan and Debian ifupdown. It refuses unsupported layouts, bridges used by virtual machines or virtual networks, and VLANs or macvlans attached to the bridge or its port. A virtual machine can block removal even when stopped.
--review checks the bridge and shows the plan without applying network changes. Without that flag, the command checks it again and starts the change. Applying settings can interrupt SSH if the bridge carries the host connection. The recovery worker continues on the host even if that connection drops.
By default, waits until the change needs confirmation or has finished. --no-wait returns the initial transaction record instead. The command never confirms automatically. Check the transaction with get-bridge-status, verify connectivity, and use confirm-bridge --id before its deadline to keep the new settings. Otherwise Cloudmin restores the previous settings. rollback-bridge requests that restoration immediately.
cloudmin remove-bridge --name br0 --review cloudmin remove-bridge --name br0 Options:
--name value: Host bridge name. --review: Show the removal plan without applying it.
heading: Moves the bridge’s network settings back to its Ethernet port

content:
cloudmin confirm-bridge [--multiline | --json] --id value Keeps the new network settings for the pending bridge transaction identified by --id. Use the transaction ID returned by the change or get-bridge-status, not the bridge name. The transaction must still be awaiting confirmation and within its deadline.
Confirm only after reconnecting and checking the host’s network access. Cloudmin performs its connectivity checks before accepting confirmation. A confirmed change no longer rolls back automatically when the original deadline passes.
To reject the change, use rollback-bridge. Once it is confirmed, that rollback command is not a general undo operation for the completed change.
cloudmin confirm-bridge --id TRANSACTION_ID Options:
--id value: Bridge transaction ID.
heading: Keeps the new network settings after checking connectivity

content:
cloudmin rollback-bridge [--multiline | --json] [--no-wait] --id value Requests restoration of the previous network settings for the bridge transaction identified by --id. Use the transaction ID from get-bridge-status. The transaction must still allow recovery; this is not an undo command for an already confirmed change.
Recovery runs on the host and can interrupt the SSH connection again as addresses move back. By default, the command waits for the transaction’s recovery result. --no-wait returns immediately; check get-bridge-status after reconnecting.
A timed-out unconfirmed change also starts automatic recovery. If recovery reports an error, inspect its status and resolve the error before submitting another bridge change.
cloudmin rollback-bridge --id TRANSACTION_ID cloudmin rollback-bridge --id TRANSACTION_ID --no-wait Options:
--id value: Bridge transaction ID.
heading: Requests recovery of the previous network settings

content:
cloudmin get-license [--multiline | --json] Shows the Cloudmin license status, expiry and any grace deadline. The license key is never returned. GPL does not require a license.
cloudmin get-license
heading: Shows the Cloudmin license status

content:
cloudmin check-license [--multiline | --json] Checks the saved license with www.virtualmin.com. Use this after renewal or after fixing a connection problem. This command remains available when license restrictions block other changes.
cloudmin check-license
heading: Rechecks the Cloudmin license with the license server

content:
cloudmin change-license [--multiline | --json] --key-file file|- --serial value Checks a new Cloudmin Pro license before saving it. Read the key from a private file or standard input. Failed validation leaves the current license in place.
cloudmin change-license --serial 12345 --key-file /root/cloudmin-key Expiry grace lasts seven days after the expiry date ends in UTC. Migration grace lasts 21 days from when this host first detects use on too many hosts. A failed check allows up to 21 days from the last successful check, without extending expiry or migration deadlines. Existing machines, accepted jobs, scheduled backups, job recovery and network rollback keep working when new changes are blocked.
Options:
--key-file file|-: License key file, or - for stdin. --serial value: Cloudmin license serial number.
heading: Validates and saves a Cloudmin Pro license

content:
cloudmin deregister-license [--multiline | --json] --yes Removes this host’s saved license and repository credentials. Running machines, scheduled backups and accepted jobs continue. Pro updates and new changes through Cloudmin require a license again. Deregistration does not cancel your subscription or immediately remove the host from the license server’s count.
cloudmin deregister-license --yes Options:
--yes: Confirm this operation.
heading: Removes this host’s Cloudmin license

content:
cloudmin api [action] < request.json Runs the raw JSON API entry point. Use cloudmin api ACTION with a JSON request object on standard input. This is useful for API fields that have no named-command option or for clients that already construct API requests. With no action, it returns options.
The raw response is a JSON object with version and result fields. Named commands use command, status and data instead. Raw errors are written to standard error and exit 1. Do not add named-command output flags such as --json or --multiline.
options, list, backups, bridges and storage need no request body. machines accepts an optional exact name or UUID selector and otherwise lists the visible inventory. Other actions take a JSON object with their documented fields. The root entry point supplies a form token when omitted, but callers remain responsible for other required fields such as revisions and confirmations.
Raw requests return their initial result without waiting for a job to finish. Use the returned job ID with get-job or the raw status action. When retrying a job submission, reuse the same request, token and attempt value so the API can return the existing job. A new named command generates a new token and submits a separate request.
Use the virtual machine API reference for action-specific JSON fields. For example, the selector file below can contain {"id":"guest.example.com"}, and the status request file can contain {"job":"JOB_ID"}. A request file is often easier to review than a long shell-quoted object. Keep files containing passwords or provider credentials private.
cloudmin api options cloudmin api machines < /root/machine-selector.json cloudmin api status < /root/job-request.json
heading: Runs the raw JSON API with a request on standard input

content:
Origin Cloudmin is made by Cloudmin LLC, the company that also sells Virtualmin Pro and our other commercial products. Our team is behind Webmin, the world’s most popular web-based Linux and UNIX system administration tool, and Virtualmin, started by Jamie Cameron and Joe Cooper in 2005. Cloudmin was announced in 2009 as a management interface for virtual machines and cloud infrastructure, built on Webmin like the rest of our products.
History The first Cloudmin generations managed Xen, KVM, OpenVZ, Solaris Zones and several public cloud providers through their own tooling and raw hypervisor processes. Over the years hosting providers and system administrators used it to run fleets of virtual machines and to provision Virtualmin servers at scale.
Cloudmin 10 is a rewrite of the product around libvirt. It manages QEMU/KVM through the standard Linux virtualization API instead of custom process management, keeps virtual hardware definitions where other tools can see them, and rebuilds images, jobs, consoles, snapshots, clones and backups on a shared core for the free and professional editions. Cloudmin 9 stays available for Xen users while the KVM line matures.
Facts Cloudmin GPL is free software and manages one host with an unlimited number of virtual machines. Cloudmin Pro adds features for people who build services at scale. Both editions share one code base, one API and one command line. Virtualmin remains a separate product, with its own GPL and Pro editions. Cloudmin is developed in the open alongside Webmin and Virtualmin, and the Virtualmin community forum is where its users and developers meet.
Us In short, we are a small team, with Eric Andreychek joining in 2008 and Ilia Rostovtsev (a.k.a. Ilia Ross) in 2014, trying to tackle really big problems in hosting and virtualization management.

Getting started with Cloudmin takes a few steps on a fresh host, using our automated install script. The script sets up your package manager, installs the Cloudmin, Webmin, libvirt and QEMU packages with their dependencies, and runs Cloudmin-Config to prepare the host for virtual machines.
Cloudmin 10 is in development
There is no stable Cloudmin 10 repository yet. The installer uses the unstable channel. Use it on test hosts, read the feature status page, and keep Cloudmin 9 for production Xen hosts. Install your operating system Start with a freshly installed supported host OS: Rocky Linux 10, AlmaLinux 10, Debian 13 or Ubuntu 26.04, on x86-64 or ARM64. The host needs CPU virtualization extensions and a working /dev/kvm. Installing inside another hypervisor works when nested virtualization is enabled. A minimal server installation is ideal; Cloudmin installs what it needs.
Don’t pre-install or pre-configure libvirt, QEMU or Webmin. The installer expects a clean supported OS and uses only the distribution’s hypervisor packages. Add third-party repositories only after installing Cloudmin, and with caution. Download and run install script Cloudmin GPL is free. Cloudmin Professional licenses are sold through the Virtualmin shop, and the Pro extension installs alongside the shared module.
Try Cloudmin Professional or Download Cloudmin GPL The quickest way to start the installation is to log in to the host over SSH and run the prepared command:
copy sudo sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://download.cloudmin.dev/cloudmin-install.sh)" Managed swap No swap The installer shows its plan, including any swap change, and asks for confirmation unless you pass --yes. Use the toggles under the command to pick the repository channel, choose how swap is handled, or switch to wget.
Install script options Run the script with --help for the full list. The most useful options:
--hostname name sets a fully qualified host name before installation. --swap SIZE, --no-swap and --swap-only control installer-managed swap. Without a size, the installer chooses one from available memory, existing swap and disk space. Unrelated swap is never removed. --no-package-updates skips the initial distribution upgrade. --extra package,... installs additional distribution packages first; --include and --exclude adjust configuration plugins. BIND and Postfix are not installed or configured by Cloudmin. --setup only configures repositories and their prerequisites. What the installer does On Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux the script enables CRB and EPEL, then installs the cloudmincore and cloudmin-kvm package groups. On Debian and Ubuntu it installs cloudmin-core and the native cloudmin-kvm-stack meta package. Dependencies are installed in one transaction, and a failed download, missing package or failed configuration step stops the installer.
Cloudmin-Config sets up Etckeeper for configuration history, then loads KVM, enables the modular libvirt daemons where they are available (or the stock libvirtd otherwise), prepares a default storage pool and a persistent NAT network, verifies the packaged EFI firmware, and configures Webmin, nftables and Fail2ban through Webmin’s own APIs. SELinux stays enforcing.
Before reporting success, the configuration boots a temporary, isolated KVM inspection appliance on the host. A failed boot stops the installation and shows the end of the configuration log. The readiness report names any missing capability and how to fix it.
After a few minutes, log in to Webmin at https://your-hostname:10000 and open Cloudmin. The overview shows the host checks, and Create Virtual Machine takes you to your first guest. See Your first virtual machine for the next steps.
Check the documentation If your host doesn’t fit these steps, see the installation documentation and host requirements. Existing Cloudmin 9 KVM hosts are not upgraded by this installer; a separate import tool with a report and rollback is planned.
Sign up for announcements To stay up to date with Cloudmin news, subscribe to the News Forum at Virtualmin.com.
